lifecycle.note: HumanLayer announced it is joining Factory on November 4, 2026. The current platform will continue during a transition of at least 30 days, with support for data export, migration to Factory or open-source self-hosting. An exact hosted shutdown date is not stated.
lifecycle.scope: Current HumanLayer hosted platform transition following the announcement that HumanLayer is joining Factory; the notice does not set an exact end date for hosted operation or open-source use.
lifecycle.continuation: HumanLayer offers open-source self-hosting as a continuation path and plans to bring its collaboration features to Factory. The announcement promises refunds for the last several months to paying customers. It does not establish that migration or self-hosting has been completed for any user.

sources.title: HumanLayer is joining Factory
sources.locator: November 4 announcement; transition period and export/migration/self-hosting paragraph

sources.title: Running a HumanLayer task
sources.locator: Before you start; installation; task and session creation
sources.finding: The tutorial uses the Apple-silicon macOS app, signed-in Claude Code, Git and an inline task. Oneshot can run directly in a checkout; other host operating systems use remote-daemon instructions. No setup timing was measured.

sources.title: How Remote Daemons Work
sources.locator: Hosts; authentication; disposable hosts; process lifecycle; browser limitations; security
sources.finding: Desktop and remote daemons run Claude/Codex on user-selected hosts. The phone/browser can start, watch and message sessions but lacks workspace configuration and embedded terminals. Long-running supervision and persisted host credentials/history are required; running sessions fail after roughly two minutes without a responding host.

sources.title: Run a remote daemon
sources.locator: Install; login or launch token; systemd; daemon updates
sources.finding: The CLI installs on the user host. Interactive device login persists credentials; launch tokens authenticate one process. A documented systemd user service or another supervisor keeps the daemon alive. npm daemons can update from the app; Windows updates manually.

sources.title: How HumanLayer tasks keep related work together
sources.locator: Task/session distinction; share and review; task files
sources.finding: Tasks group separately configured sessions and shared files. Editors add sessions and edit files; reviewers comment. Supported agent file tools sync text, HTML, images and PDFs into the artifact view, including across workstations. This is not a repository backup.

sources.title: Workspace setup
sources.locator: Before you start; Configure with agent; checks; troubleshooting
sources.finding: Workspace setup uses local Git repositories, branches and one or several task worktrees. A configuration skill proposes shared/local JSON, source refs, setup commands and files to copy. Failed setup can require manual diagnosis.

sources.title: How workspace configuration works
sources.locator: Primary repository; effective configuration; task workspace
sources.finding: Shared and local JSON configure separate worktrees for each repository; setup commands and copied files apply per repository. Skills/instructions load across repositories, while MCP and Claude settings follow the launch directory.

sources.title: Run a workflow in HumanLayer
sources.locator: Select workflow; phases; changing plans; finish
sources.finding: Oneshot, RPI, PRD-Oriented and Freeform are distinct paths. Users review and amend saved artifacts; later artifacts take precedence. PR creation is a separate skill/action. Freeform has no fixed phases.

sources.title: Skills and workflows reference
sources.locator: Workflow choices; artifact precedence; checkpoints; implementation; PR output; auto-advance
sources.finding: RPI skills create and revise task artifacts, split implementation into checked phases and use manual or selected automatic handoffs. PR skills compare the branch diff with the plan, create/update a PR and save a description or optional walkthrough. These are documented agent workflows, not verified delivery enforcement.

sources.title: Sub-agent models and effort
sources.locator: Claude Code and Codex tables; Faster Research Subagents; exclusions
sources.finding: RPI uses named research/implementation subagents with harness-specific model/effort rules. Claude uses fixed model aliases or inherit; Codex children use the parent model with role-specific effort. Experiments control faster research; project/user definitions can differ.

sources.title: Set Up Codex CLI
sources.locator: Authentication; custom Responses endpoint; select model/effort
sources.finding: The HumanLayer CLI supports Codex browser/device authentication, configurable OpenAI Responses, Bedrock and Azure endpoints, model selection and reasoning effort. Endpoint credentials and model compatibility have explicit restrictions.

sources.title: Route models through an LLM gateway
sources.locator: Gateway and provider configuration
sources.finding: Documents user-configured model gateways/proxies; endpoint settings and daemon environment determine the provider route. This is distinct from a universal harness adapter or a verified local-model setup.

sources.title: Connect GitHub and Create Tasks from Issues
sources.locator: Install permissions; create task; source-issue artifact links
sources.finding: Organization admins connect repository-scoped GitHub Apps. Issue details/comments enter ticket.md, and artifact links update one source-issue comment. Failed link updates do not block saving an artifact.

sources.title: Connect Linear and Run Ticket Workflows
sources.locator: Create task; RPI workflow states; CLI
sources.finding: Linear OAuth imports issues and synchronizes named workflow states and artifact links. The separate Linear CLI can inspect/manage states and update issues; this is external issue management.

sources.title: Connect Jira and Create Tasks from Tickets
sources.locator: Before you start; create and check task
sources.finding: Organization admins authorize Jira Cloud. Tasks can start from accessible tickets; reconnect/disconnect and import toggles are documented. It does not establish complete two-way field synchronization.

sources.title: Run HumanLayer Sessions in Automations
sources.locator: How it works; tasks/sessions; personal access token; GitHub Actions
sources.finding: automation run creates/reuses a task and runs one Cloud-visible session in a user-supplied CI/cron checkout. It uses a PAT and provider credentials, starts a job-local daemon with permission prompts bypassed, streams events and exits with session result. Scheduling, concurrency and no-op guards belong to the external workflow.

sources.title: HumanLayer release notes
sources.finding: Recent releases add directory-task worktrees, multiplayer beta UI, orchestration/teleport skills, Pi streaming, diff comments and attention notifications. Earlier entries document live shared drafts, harness handoff, public review links, usage-limit recovery, host load and opt-in GitHub PR controls.

sources.title: HumanLayer platform and pricing
sources.locator: Starter; Pro; Enterprise; FAQ; Security
sources.finding: Starter advertises up to three members and 200 sessions/month. Pro is USD 100/user/month with BYO subscriptions/API keys; Enterprise lists SSO/SAML and a SOC 2 Type II assertion. The undated open-source FAQ is stale relative to the October 23 announcement; pricing is read in the November 4 transition context.

sources.title: Open sourcing HumanLayer
sources.locator: October 23; what is inside; running it yourself
sources.finding: The vendor identifies the current desktop/web application, daemon/CLI, API and sync proxy as Apache-2.0 core matching Cloud. Self-hosting setup still requires third-party keys; future deployment guides remain plans. Self-build telemetry is disabled unless configured.

sources.title: HumanLayer README.md
sources.locator: What is here; get started; self-hosting; license
sources.finding: The pinned current application repository includes desktop/web, daemon, CLI and server components and supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Pi. It identifies Electron/Tauri macOS shells, a local devstack and telemetry controls through unset environment configuration.

sources.title: HumanLayer LICENSE

sources.title: HumanLayer apps/riptide-humanlayer-claude-plugin/skills/orchestrate/SKILL.md
sources.locator: Job table and rules
sources.finding: The built-in orchestration skill uses the HumanLayer CLI to choose hosts, launch tasks and sessions, inspect statuses/PRs and manage task artifacts. This is a product-supplied skill, not evidence of an independently tested cross-harness team.

sources.title: HumanLayer apps/riptide-humanlayer-claude-plugin/skills/orchestrate/references/list-tasks.md
sources.locator: Task list and session status table
sources.finding: The CLI lists persistent task IDs/slugs, owner filters and archive metadata. This reference explicitly says a task has no status of its own; draft/running/needs-approval/usage-limit/failed states belong to sessions.

sources.title: HumanLayer apps/riptide-humanlayer-claude-plugin/skills/orchestrate/references/launch-task.md
sources.locator: Project and workspace-spec launch; setup checks
sources.finding: CLI examples create the same task/workspace UUID and launch sessions, including tasks without external tickets. Repository materialization/errors are inspectable; copy/setup command errors need not block launch. Existing-folder execution is allowed explicitly.

sources.title: HumanLayer apps/riptide-humanlayer-claude-plugin/skills/orchestrate/references/launch-session.md
sources.locator: Launch in project; choices for both
sources.finding: CLI examples launch sessions under a task ID, configure host/agent/model and choose default, accept_edits, auto or bypass permissions. Another host uses the pushed task branch; unpushed work stays behind.

sources.title: HumanLayer apps/cli/src/api/proxy-router.ts
sources.locator: EXCLUDED_ROUTE_GROUPS; applySyncDefaults; createProxyRouter
sources.finding: The CLI proxies the product RPC contract except metrics and requires scoped filters for conversation-event sync. This supports product-owned API access, not a stability guarantee or an exposed MCP server.

sources.title: HumanLayer Claude provider login driver
sources.locator: apps/riptide-daemon/src/effects/services/provider-login/drivers/claude-login-driver.ts lines 34-88 (AUTH_LOGIN_ARGS, runLogin), commit f9bd735
sources.finding: The daemon's Claude sign-in spawns the installed Claude Code CLI with `auth login` / `auth status`, so the CLI's own account login (including subscription sign-in) is used; the Codex driver separately runs ChatGPT device sign-in.

sources.title: HumanLayer Claude session launch
sources.locator: apps/riptide-daemon/src/effects/services/claude-sessions/prepare-claude-session.ts lines 172-176 (locateClaudeExecutable; pathToClaudeCodeExecutable at line 384), commit f9bd735
sources.finding: Claude sessions locate the user's installed claude executable (configured path or PATH) and pass it to the Agent SDK as pathToClaudeCodeExecutable, so sessions run on the local Claude Code install and its login.

sources.title: HumanLayer release notes 0.149.0
sources.locator: apps/docs/release-notes.md lines 675-692 (0.149.0, July 27, 2026, Other Changes), commit f9bd735
sources.finding: Release 0.149.0 notes that task and session lists were stabilised so rows stop reshuffling while agents run in parallel, i.e. several sessions run at once in the shipped app.

sources.locator: apps/riptide-humanlayer-claude-plugin/skills/orchestrate/references/list-tasks.md lines 1-10 (list-tasks reference), commit f9bd735
sources.finding: The bundled orchestration reference states that a task has no status of its own; only its sessions carry statuses. Tasks can be listed, paged, filtered by owner and archived.

sources.title: HumanLayer remote daemons explanation
sources.locator: apps/docs/explanation/remote-daemons.md lines 66-113 (Daemon hosts; Containers; Disposable and suspended hosts), commit f9bd735
sources.finding: A daemon host can be a cloud VM, workstation or private-network machine, and the docs explain running the daemon inside a container (credential volume) and on disposable/suspended VMs. The daemon is the host; the docs do not describe HumanLayer creating a container or VM per session.

sources.title: HumanLayer desktop versioning
sources.locator: apps/riptide-native/README.md lines 11-13 (Versioning), commit f9bd735
sources.finding: Desktop releases derive their version at build time and every merge to main ships a new auto-updated version, so the pinned main commit corresponds to shipped builds (GitHub Releases only hold old codelayer pre-releases).
